thread.title: Markets Rally as GM, Micron Gain on Earnings

author: Barron's
title: Markets Rally as GM, Micron Gain on Earnings
text:
Update: Scratch that. The market has opened and it's trading higher as of 9:52 a.m. today. The S&P 500 has gained 0.7% to 2666.95, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average has advanced 98.03 points, or 0.4%, to 24,443.78. The Nasdaq Composite has risen 0.5% to 7003.40.
Here's the original post. The commentary still stands, even if the market moves have changed.
Original Post: A market that just over a week ago could do nothing but go up now does nothing but go down.
Getty Images S&P 500 futures have dropped 1%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures have tumbled 311 points, or 1.3%. Nasdaq Composite futures have fallen 1%. These numbers, however, may be unreliable in determining where the market will open because of the mechanics of futures trading and computing "fair value."]
[ Editors note: Market's have gotten a bid this morning since publication. At 8:59 a.m. today, the Dow is down 117 points, or 0.5%, while S&P 500 futures are up 0.1% and Nasdaq Composite futures have risen 0.3%. Expect these numbers to fluctuate.
When I wrote that we were in the midst of a correction over the weekend, I didn't expect it to pick up this kind of steam this quickly. And looking across the market, I'm not sure anyone else did either. But as of this morning--with the SPDR S&P 500 ETF down 1.8% at $259.40--we're looking at a correction occurring in just seven days from Jan 26, when the market was at an all-time high.
And so strategists are coming out with their recommendations--and many seem to be reluctantly buying the dip. SunTrust's Keith Lerner, for instance, writes that he would "would lean into this weakness as opposed to selling into it." JPMorgan's Dubravko Lakos-Bujas writes that he sees "the market selloff entirely disconnected from fundamentals." And RBC's Lori Calvasina writes that she sees "more positives than negatives for US equities," and that for now "we are buyers on the dip."
Aren't we all.
Becton Dickinson ( BDX ) has dropped 6.1% to $211 despite reporting a profit of $2.48 a share, besting the Street consensus for $2.41 cents, on sales of $3.08, beating analyst estimates for $3.05 billion. The company also said it would earn between $10.85 and $11.00 in 2018. Analysts had been predicting $10.88.
Cirrus Logic ( CRUS ) has tumbled 13% to $39.10 after reporting a third-quarter profit of $1.59 a share, missing forecasts for $1.78 a share, on sales of $482.7 million, well below analyst expectations for $529.4 million. "When a single customer is 86% of corporate revenues, one can expect quarterly volatility," writes Needham analyst Rajvindra Gill.
Dunkin' Brands ( DNKN ) has fallen 1.4% to $60 after reporting a profit of 64 cents a share , besting analyst expectations by a penny. Sales came in at $227.1 million, ahead of forecasts for $220.6 million. The company did not offer guidance. "DNKN remains a solid name in the sector in our view, and we still believe DNKN is in a good position to sustain at least low-to-mid-teen EPS growth," writes Maxim analyst Stephen Anderson. "We thus recommend buying DNKN on any weakness as broader markets stabilize."
General Motors ( GM ) has risen 1.6% to $40.17 after reporting a profit of $1.65 a share , topping analyst forecasts for $1.38, on sales of $37.7 billion, ahead of expectations for $36.55 billion.
Getty Images Lennox International ( LII ) has climbed 2.8% to $201.50 after reporting a fourth-quarter profit of $1.68 a share on sales of $892 million. Analysts had been predicting earnings of r $1.65 a share on revenue of $906.5 million. Lennox also raised its full-year guidance to a range of $9.75 to $10.35, ahead of forecasts for $9.45.
lululemon athletica (LULU) has dropped 2.5% to $75.50 after the surprise resignation of its CEO, who "fell short [the company's] standards of conduct. "We continue to see LULU at an inflection point in its product momentum, global growth, and leadership position in technology, and see upside opportunity to earnings in 2018," writes MKM analyst Roxanne Meyer. "We would view any weakness associated with this announcement as an opportunity to buy the stock."
Micron Technology (MU) has gained 2.5% to $40.39 after forecasting a fiscal second-quarter profit of $2.70 to $2.75 a share on revenue between $7.20 billion and $7.35 billion. Analysts had been predicting earnings of $2.58 a share on revenue of $7.02 billion. "MU remains at a crossroads and key questions remain, revolving around: CFO priorities, MU's cost positioning, long-term FCF generation, System-level capabilities, capex investment and M&A," writes Susquehanna analyst Mehdi Hosseini.
Tapestry (TPR) has jumped 5% to $47.21 after reporting a second-quarter profit of $1.07 cents a share , bearing forecasts for 89 cents a share, on sales of $1.79 billion, narrowly topping estimates for $1.77 billion. The company formerly known as Coach also said it would earn between $2.52 and $2.60 in fiscal 2018, above forecasts for $2.41. "We continue to view TPR as a largely unprecedented brand transformation that reflects the strength of management, ability to execute, and the power of innovation," writes MKM analyst Roxanne Meyer.
Dr Pepper Snapple Group (DPS) has risen 1.1% to $119.67 after getting raised to Overweight from Equal Weight at Barclays.
ExxonMobil (XOM) has fallen 1.2% to $78.80 after getting cut to Underweight from Overweight at Barclays. Barclays upgraded Chevron (CVX) to Overweight from Equal Weight, but that hasn't helped the stock, which has dropped 1.4% to $111.
You're going to be hearing a lot about how this is a normal correction . There's nothing normal about it.
Getty Images I don't mean there's anything nefarious going on, or that we should blame machines for creating a bigger move than it would have been otherwise. What I do mean is that markets have rarely, if ever, gone from a new all-time high to a nearly 10% correction in such a short period of time. It's as if we were cruising along in a Ferrari only to accidentally go into reverse at an even faster speed.
But that's pretty much what has happened. Sundial Capital Research's Jason Goepfert notes that there have been three times when the S&P 500 declined in following after going 370 days or more without a 5% decline from its peak: In 1965, 1994, and 1996. The ends of those streaks were followed by quick drops--of 9.6% over 31 days; of 8.9% in 42 days; and of 7.6% in 34 days. That's what a normal correction looks like. "Monday's trading - and post-close moves - are the types of action only seen a few times in history," he says.
It's that speed of the drop, and not the drop itself that makes this correction something out of the ordinary.
The stock market is in free-fall but a prominent Silicon Valley venture capitalist sees nothing but upside for tech IPOs and M&As this year.
"I'm really bullish on the (tech) sector," Sandy Miller, general partner at VC firm IVP, said on a sun-splashed Monday morning that matched his outlook. "I expect a good IPO market, as a subset of exits" that include plenty of mergers and acquisitions.
Bloomberg News Tech giants flush with cash hoards -- Apple (AAPL), Amazon.com (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT) and Facebook (FB) - will "fill out their grids" in product areas of need without fear of anti-trust repercussions because they're all "getting bigger and bigger," Miller said.
Miller anticipates a robust year for exit strategies that go beyond traditional means. He predicts more private companies will explore so-called "dual tracking," a strategy popularized by software company AppDynamics, which was acquired by Cisco Systems (CSCO) for $3.7 billion shortly before its scheduled IPO last year. With more cash available because of the U.S. tax bill, Miller believes private companies can choose to pursue an IPO while at the same time listening to acquisition offers.
More companies might also mirror Spotify's direct listing in lieu of a conventional IPO. The online music service, which has plenty of name recognition, doesn't need to burnish its brand name, says Miller, a former investment banker.
"I don't expect a lot of companies" to pursue a direct listing, Miller said in an interview at the later-stage firm's headquarters on bucolic Sand Hill Road. "But the visible (well-known) ones will."
At the very least, he anticipates an improvement in the number of tech IPOs , and amount raised, after several subpar years. But there is one forthcoming IPO he's mum about: Dropbox, in which IVP is an investor.
